content: The Muir Department of Water and Sanitation in South Africa, represented by Angeline Mulwa from the University of Nairobi, Kenya, collaborates with Anna Murray from the Aquaya Institute in the USA. Edirida Musinguzi from the Ministry of Water and Environment in Uganda, Peter Mutale from the National Water Supply and Sanitation Council in Zambia, and Jackline Muturi from Eawag in Switzerland also contribute to this initiative. Thorsteinn Narfason from Environmental and Public Health West Iceland, Ray Norman from World Vision International in the USA, and Ronald Nyakana from the Ministry of Water and Environment in Uganda are key participants. Rajit Ojha from the Ministry of Water Supply in Nepal, Li Ong from the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom, and Emmanuel Opong, formerly of World Vision International in Eswatini, are also involved. Olayinka Osuolale from Elizade University in Nigeria, Marc Overmars from UNICEF in Zimbabwe, and Sudan Raj Panthi from WHO in Nepal provide their expertise. Rachel Peletz from the Aquaya Institute in the USA, Richard Phillips from the Drinking Water Inspectorate in the United Kingdom, and Oscar Pintos from Asociación Federal de Entes Reguladores de Agua y Saneamiento in Argentina are notable contributors. Diego Pixcar from Water For People in Guatemala, Adam Questad from World Vision in the USA, and Claude Ramseier, formerly of UNICEF in the USA, also play significant roles. Jarkko Rapala from the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health in Finland, Andrea Rechenburg from the University of Bonn in Germany, and Joselito Riego de Dios from the Department of Health in the Philippines are part of this effort. James Robertson from UNICEF Pacific Multi-Country Office in Fiji, Michelle Roche from the Environmental Protection Agency in Ireland, and Susana Rodrigues from the Water and Waste Services Regulation Authority in Portugal are also involved. Jan Willem Rosenboom, formerly of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation in the USA, Kenneth Rotert from the United States Environmental Protection Agency, and Ion Salaru from the National Centre of Public Health in the Republic of Moldova contribute their expertise. Aline Saraiva from Skat Foundation in Switzerland, Samuel Schlesinger from Green Empowerment in Ecuador, and Joanna Seto from the Hawaii State Department of Health in the USA are also key participants. Karen Setty from the Aquaya Institute in the USA, Andrew Shantz, a consultant in Cambodia, and Jesse Shapiro from USAID in the USA are involved. Esther Shaylor from UNICEF in Denmark, Kari Sholtes from the University of Colorado Boulder in the USA, and Raja Ram Pote Shrestha from WHO in Nepal are contributors. Worlanyo Kwadjo Siabi from the Community Water and Sanitation Agency in Ghana, Olga Slepner from the Governmental Authority for Water and Sewage in Israel, and Theingi Soe from UNICEF Pacific Multi-Country Office in Vanuatu are also part of this initiative. Philip Songa from Arup in the United Kingdom, Sabrina Sorlini from the University of Brescia in Italy, and Johan Strandberg from WHO in Switzerland contribute their expertise. Pierre Studer, formerly of UNICEF in the USA, Sally Sutton from SWL Consultants in the United Kingdom, and Sochettra Tang from WHO in Cambodia are also involved. Gassama Amadou Tidiane, formerly of World Vision International in Senegal, Rowland Titus, a consultant in the United Republic of Tanzania, and Chiranjibi Tiwari from UNICEF in Nigeria are key participants. Obinna Uche from UNICEF in Nigeria, Sital Uprety from Eawag in Switzerland, and Koenraad Vancraeynest from UNICEF in Mozambique are also contributors. Márta Vargha from the National Public Health Centre in Hungary, Bisrantee Wagle, formerly of WHO in Switzerland, and Juliet Willetts from the University of Technology of Sydney in Australia are involved in this effort. This document has also benefited from the insights of numerous experts and practitioners from the Rural Water Supply Network and the WHO International Network of Drinking-water and Sanitation Regulators (RegNet), as well as participants in various international meetings and conferences. Members of WHO’s Drinking-water Quality Committee for the fourth edition of WHO’s Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality are acknowledged for their contributions. Rod Shaw from Loughborough University in the United Kingdom provided technical illustrations and advice related to sanitary inspection tools. WHO expresses gratitude for the financial support provided by the Agence Française de Développement in France, the Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation in the USA, the Directorate General for International Cooperation in the Netherlands, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office in the United Kingdom, the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs in Luxembourg, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare in Japan, and the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation in Norway. The Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality: Small Water Supplies emphasize the importance of providing access to safe and adequate drinking-water services as a means to promote health and reduce poverty. Small water supplies play a critical role in meeting this need, as they serve a significant proportion of the global population, particularly in rural areas, small towns, peri-urban areas, and urban areas. However, small water supplies are more likely to face challenges related to water safety, which can lead to water-related illnesses and adverse social and economic impacts. Improving the management and performance of small water supplies offers an opportunity to enhance public health, address inequalities, and improve livelihoods. These guidelines aim to address the needs and opportunities associated with small water supplies to facilitate progressive improvements toward safe and sustainable drinking-water services for all. The guidelines are intended to assist governments and practitioners in improving the safety of drinking water delivered through small supplies. They are primarily directed at decision-makers at national and subnational levels responsible for developing and implementing drinking-water quality regulatory frameworks and associated risk management and surveillance programs. Other stakeholders involved in water service provision, including non-governmental organizations and community-based organizations, will also benefit from the guidance. The guidelines are also relevant for small water suppliers, although most recommendations are directed at the institutions that regulate and support them. The guidelines are based on the principal recommendation in WHO’s Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality, which emphasizes a framework for safe drinking water. They provide guidance on applying this recommendation to small water supplies, including water quality targets, water safety planning, and independent surveillance to ensure effective risk management practices and health-based targets are met. The guidelines are complemented by WHO’s 2024 Sanitary Inspection Packages, which support the implementation of these guidelines. Sanitary inspection is a simple, on-site evaluation using a checklist to identify risk factors that may lead to water supply contamination. Together, these resources update and supersede WHO’s 1997 Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality. The guidelines highlight the importance of preventive risk management, tailored guidance for diverse small water supplies, and recommendations targeting decision-makers. They cover a wide range of small water supplies, including household-managed supplies, community-managed supplies, and professionally managed supplies. The guidelines establish a reference typology of small water supplies based on management models to support practical and risk-based guidance. Users of the guidelines are encouraged to consider their specific contexts and apply the recommendations accordingly. The document outlines ten guiding principles foundational to improving drinking-water safety in small supplies, including prioritizing public health, adopting a risk-based approach, progressively improving services, adapting to context, strengthening systems, engaging water suppliers, practicing supportive regulation, approaching water, sanitation, and hygiene holistically, providing equitable services, and building climate resilience. Concrete actions to apply these principles are presented in the guidelines, along with six key recommendations for achieving safe services from small water supplies. These include assessing the enabling environment, engaging and supporting small water suppliers, promoting catchment-to-consumer risk management, defining priority water quality parameters, and developing strategic plans to strengthen the enabling environment.
